\chapter{Water and Rice}
\label{ch:ta-water-and-rice}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for water and keep raw \ta{அரிசி} apart from cooked \ta{சாதம்}, and state how far the arisi-to-\textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{} claim can honestly be pushed.}

Assemble taṇ plus nīr into taṇṇīr, switch between arisi and sātam by whether it is cooked, and label the English \textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{} link as contested.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{தண்ணீர்} \ta{அரிசி} \ta{சாதம்}]{\ta{தண்ணீர்}, \ta{அரிசி}, \ta{சாதம்} — water, and rice, the real staple}

\label{lesson:TA-C15-thanneer-arisi}



\begin{quote}
European languages teach \textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{} as the staple food. Here, that would be \textbf{dishonest} — bread isn't the everyday staple in Tamil food culture. \textbf{Rice} is, and it comes with one of the most famous (if contested) etymological journeys of any food-word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தண்ணீர்} — water, literally \textquotedblleft{}cool water\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ta{தண்ணீர்}} (\emph{taṇṇīr}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{water}\textquotedblright{} — built from \textbf{\ta{தண்}} (\emph{taṇ}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cool}\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{நீர்}} (\emph{nīr}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{water}\textquotedblright{}). Everyday Tamil doesn't just say \textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{} — it says, quite literally, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cool water}.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அரிசி} and \ta{சாதம்} — rice, raw and cooked}
Tamil, like most of South India, distinguishes the \textbf{uncooked grain} from the \textbf{cooked dish} with two separate words, not one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{அரிசி}} (\emph{arisi}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rice}\textquotedblright{} (the raw, husked grain) — native Dravidian.
  \item \textbf{\ta{சாதம்}} (\emph{sātam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cooked rice}\textquotedblright{} (the meal itself, what's actually eaten) — likely Sanskrit-influenced. Tamil also keeps a native word for the same idea, \textbf{\ta{சோறு}} (\emph{cōṟu}) — the two sit side by side as everyday near-synonyms.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Here's the exciting part, held with appropriate care: many etymologists connect \textbf{\ta{அரிசி}} (\emph{arisi}) to the \textbf{English word \textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{} itself} — the proposed chain runs Dravidian \emph{arisi} $\to$ \textbf{Greek} \emph{óryza} $\to$ Latin \emph{oryza} $\to$ Old French \emph{ris} $\to$ English \textbf{rice}. If true, English speakers have been saying a Dravidian word for centuries without knowing it. But be honest: standard etymological dictionaries mark Greek \emph{óryza}'s origin as \textbf{genuinely uncertain} — a Dravidian source is one widely cited hypothesis among others (an Indo-Aryan \emph{vrīhi}-related source is also proposed), not a settled, universally agreed fact.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}taṇ\textquotedblright{} — cool — then \textquotedblleft{}nīr,\textquotedblright{} water — then \textquotedblleft{}taṇṇīr,\textquotedblright{} cool water
  \item \textquotedblleft{}arisi\textquotedblright{} — raw rice — then \textquotedblleft{}sātam,\textquotedblright{} cooked rice
  \item the famous (contested) link — \textquotedblleft{}arisi\textquotedblright{} $\to$ possibly English \textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ta{தண்ணீர்}} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Cool water\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{taṇ} \textquotedblleft{}cool\textquotedblright{} + \emph{nīr} \textquotedblleft{}water.\textquotedblright{}) What two words does Tamil use for rice, and why two? (\textbf{\ta{அரிசி}} \emph{arisi}, raw grain; \textbf{\ta{சாதம்}} \emph{sātam}, cooked rice — the raw grain and the cooked meal get separate words.) Is it certain that English \textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{} comes from Tamil \emph{arisi}? (\textbf{Not certain} — it's a widely cited hypothesis via Greek \emph{óryza}, but that Greek word's origin is genuinely disputed among etymologists.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\ta{அ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-S119-letter-a}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ta{ட} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{அ}}
\textbf{\ta{அ}} — \emph{a}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{a} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a curl at the upper left
  \item a long horizontal stroke
  \item a straight vertical on the right
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \ta{அ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{அப்பா} \ta{அம்மா} \ta{அண்ணன்} \ta{தம்பி} \ta{அக்கா} \ta{தங்கை}} — father, mother, and FOUR sibling words
  \item \textbf{\ta{தண்ணீர்} \ta{அரிசி} \ta{சாதம்}} — water, and rice — the actual staple food here, not bread — with a widely-cited
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{அ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start inside the upper curl and sweep around it
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, continue down the outer curve
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, turn around the lower loop
  \item \textbf{4.} without lifting, carry the horizontal to the right edge — then lift once
  \item \textbf{5.} set the pen at the top of the separate right upright and draw straight down
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The pen comes up 1 time and no more.

\begin{quote}
Two strokes — four joined movements, one pen lift, then the right upright; cited to Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Frame 4, \ta{அ}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 4, \ta{அ} (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 192.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ta{அ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{அ} three times, saying \emph{a} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ta{அ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{அ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
